title: Asking Data Questions in Plain Language
answer: Asking data questions in plain language means a person types a question such as "which regions grew fastest last quarter" and a system translates it into a query against a database, spreadsheet, or data warehouse. It sits in quantitative analysis and reproducible work because the answer must be traceable to the same data and definitions each time. The practice covers text to SQL, semantic search over tables, and natural language interfaces to business intelligence tools. It is not a replacement for knowing the data model, but a way to lower the first step of exploration.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Asking data questions in plain language means a person types a question such as "which regions grew fastest last quarter" and a system translates it into a query against a database, spreadsheet, or data warehouse. It sits in quantitative analysis and reproducible work because the answer must be traceable to the same data and definitions each time. The practice covers text to SQL, semantic search over tables, and natural language interfaces to business intelligence tools. It is not a replacement for knowing the data model, but a way to lower the first step of exploration.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A working setup needs a data source with a documented schema, a semantic layer or data dictionary that maps business terms to columns, and a query engine that can execute the generated code. Many teams use a large language model to draft SQL or another query language, then a validator checks syntax and permissions before execution. The result appears in a table, chart, or notebook cell, often with the generated query shown for inspection. Reproducibility depends on versioned schemas, saved queries, and a record of the model and prompt used.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The analyst starts with a clear question, confirms the relevant tables and metrics, and lets the system propose a query. They review the query for joins, filters, and aggregations, then run it against a read only copy or a controlled environment. The answer is compared with a known result or a manual check, and the query is saved with the question and the data version. Over time, teams build a library of verified question and query pairs to improve accuracy and reduce repeated mistakes.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Plain language access can expose sensitive rows if permissions are not enforced at the query layer. Every generated query should carry the identity of the asker, the source tables, the time of execution, and the model version that produced it. Provenance means the original question, the translated query, and the result stay linked so a reviewer can replay the path. Teams also need rules for ambiguous terms, because "revenue" or "active user" may have several definitions. The site's library holds 135 research papers, and its content links to the original paper rather than a search tool, which is a reminder to keep the source visible.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect tighter integration with notebooks, version control, and data catalogues so that a plain language question becomes a reproducible artifact. Evaluation will move from "did it run" to "did it match the agreed metric definition" and "can another analyst get the same answer." Smaller, domain specific models and semantic layers may handle common questions without sending data to an external service. The field will keep a human in the loop for high stakes numbers, with the plain language layer acting as an entry point rather than the final authority.
